content: Individuals with neuromuscular disorders often experience a weak and ineffective cough, which increases their susceptibility to respiratory complications. Cough augmentation techniques are designed to enhance the effectiveness of coughing, facilitate mucus clearance, reduce the frequency and duration of respiratory infections that necessitate hospital admissions, and ultimately improve the quality of life for these patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various cough augmentation techniques in both adults and children with chronic neuromuscular disorders. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted on April 13, 2020, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and randomized cross-over trials. The inclusion criteria for the review encompassed studies that compared cough augmentation techniques to no treatment, alternative techniques, or combinations of techniques in individuals with chronic neuromuscular disorders. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the trials, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The primary outcomes of interest were the number and duration of unscheduled hospitalizations due to acute respiratory exacerbations. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 11 studies involving a total of 287 participants, ranging in age from 3 to 73 years. The studies examined various cough augmentation techniques, including manually assisted cough, mechanical insufflation, manual and mechanical breath-stacking, mechanical insufflation-exsufflation, glossopharyngeal breathing, and combination techniques. These were compared to unassisted coughing as well as alternative or sham interventions. However, none of the included studies reported data on the primary outcomes of the review, namely the number and duration of unscheduled hospital admissions. Additionally, adverse events were not listed as either primary or secondary outcome measures in any of the studies. The evidence suggests that certain cough augmentation techniques may improve peak cough flow when compared to unassisted coughing (based on data from 199 participants across 8 RCTs). However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. Furthermore, there appears to be little to no difference in peak cough flow outcomes when comparing different cough augmentation techniques to one another (based on data from 216 participants across 9 RCTs). There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions regarding the effects of these interventions on other important outcomes, such as measures of gaseous exchange, pulmonary function, quality of life, general functional status, or participant preference and satisfaction. In conclusion, the safety and efficacy of cough augmentation techniques in adults and children with chronic neuromuscular disorders remain highly uncertain. Further well-designed studies are necessary to provide more definitive evidence on their clinical utility.
